So the number of people who do not have elementary school education is 30 per cent. So you haven't even bothered to be consistent in your own report so as not to repeat different pieces of information and figures in different places. What does this mean then, that 30 per cent of the population have not completed elementary school? A moment ago you said 46 per cent were illiterate, and neither of those figures are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, answer that question it you would, and that will conclude the cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I relied on several sources, including Nicole du Roy. I also used -- for numbers which would show the importance and weight of television and its impact on the population which was not familiar -- was not used to reading a great deal, I relied on several figures. Specifically as regards the weight of television, since it was the main medium covering Serbian territory and therefore the principal information or news medium for most of the population, I would refer to a report prepared in about -- which was about the elections in Serbia in 1990 through 2000 that were prepared by two fellows from the University of Belgrade called: "Television Elections and -- Elections in Serbia, 1990 to 2000, TV images in government and opposition". The study was done by Jovanka Matic. Jovanka Matic. And by Snezana Milojevic, and it is based on figures provided by RTS television at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, just a couple of questions more. You told me I had another two or -- you didn't say I had two or three questions left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've really had sufficient time on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've consulted. My colleagues think you should have two more questions, and literally that, otherwise we shall never finish this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is one question, please. To make it clear to you, I have taken out of the binder that you have provided me for Mr. Kristan, this is Borba, a federal newspaper, dated of the 17th of March. The opposing side, in its opening statement, said that on that occasion I said that Yugoslavia was dead, and the sentence that is clearly quoted here says: "The Presidency of SFRY has not been functioning for a long time, and the illusion of the efforts of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and the efforts which in fact are lacking as of tonight are definitely dead." So I'm saying that the illusion regarding the efforts of the Presidency are dead because it fell apart, whereas the opposing side said that I had said that Yugoslavia was dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you're an expert for the media, the question is: Do you consider this to be a manipulation if I say that an illusion that there are efforts which are -- do not exist are dead, is it a manipulation if I am alleged to have said that Yugoslavia was dead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a question for the witness. You can -- you can ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, I gave you a hundred pages of various different non-Yugoslav articles, articles that were not published in Serbia, and I have another one of the 31st of December, 1999, referring to the witness Barani who testified here, saying that his allegations were investigated, that it was established that they were not true, and it ends with the quotation: "Mr. Barani doesn't completely stand by his story. 'I told everybody that was a supposition. It was not confirmed information,' he says, [In English] 'But he says for the Serbs everything is possible.'" So these fabricated falsehoods and everything that you read in those 100 pages, would you have made somewhat different conclusions if you had consulted all those sources instead of your own selective sources which show that you did not make a study of the contents of the media reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness need not answer because it's totally irrelevant, a report about Mr. Barani. It's nothing to do with the witness at all. Just a moment, please. But, Mr. de la Brosse, you should have the opportunity of commenting on the articles we invited you to look at which the accused produced to you on the last occasion you were here. So if you have any comments on them, this is the time to make them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consulted -- well, I went through all of these press excerpts, mostly from the international press, and I had several problems in respect of the nature and status of the excerpts from the various newspapers because there is no information about the author's status. We don't know whether it's an article by one person or some of the texts are in quotation marks, others are not. So I would simply like to point out the difficulty I would have in reacting to this type of text by giving you one example, the one of page 13, which is an article by Thomas Fleiner that was published in a Swiss newspaper in German, the Die Welt Woche, and the name of it has to do with demonisation of a people in 1994. The article is in quotations. Nothing is known about the author, and so I took the initiative and I did some research into the author, and I tried to find the article. It turns out that I was able to find a document by Thomas Fleiner which can be found on a Serbian site. I could give you the Internet address if we put the document on the -- the ELMO. And the text which is published by an academician in Switzerland and it's about ten pages long, the excerpt that it was suggested I comment on is presented as an ordinary speech which in fact does not correspond with reality, because in the text which you see on the Internet site which has the entire speech, when you -- I was asked to comment on the first part. The beginning of the text comes from the second page of the work of this academician. And then the -- I was also asked to look at something which appears on page 5, and it goes on to page 6 and then goes on to page 8 and further yet to page 10. In the article that I was asked to comment on, nothing is said about the fact that the article, about the pieces of the article come from different passage of a text that was prepared by an academician which in itself is problematical because I'm not sure that by working that way we are respecting the author's thoughts, and it seems to me they were rather distorting the intention and the demonstration made by that author. In particular when we're dealing with an article whose purpose was to see to what extent the multi-ethnic experience in Switzerland can be used to investigate matters in the Balkans. There are certain positions taken by the author particularly in favour of pluralism in the media within Yugoslavia, and that leaves doubts with me in respect of the meaning to be given to the author's text if I compare what I was asked to compare with the entire text, and so I would have difficulty in commenting on that type of text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, plainly if we are to introduce these -- No. You've been on long enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can address us at the end. If we are going to admit any of these articles, plainly we should not admit excerpts, we should admit the whole article because otherwise the meaning can be distorted. But we'll consider that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can address that at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have an objection, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can make it at the end. You've gone on long enough today. Let Mr. Tapuskovic cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I really did do my best to select a topic from the vast subjects that could be discussed here, so I have selected three or four which I consider to be of importance for your -- the Judges' deliberation was respect to all the problems before you, Your Honours. So I really would ask you to allot me some time to go through them. I'll be as quick as possible. And if Mr. de la Brosse gives me yes or no answers wherever possible, that would be a great help. I think I will be able to get through my questions very quickly. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. de la Brosse, let me start off from paragraph 111, if I may, and that is towards the end of your report, in fact. Perhaps I won't have time to yet through everything I wish to get through, but it is a paragraph which is titled or, rather, first of all, it was entitled "The impossibility of a democratic political alternative." That was the first title. And then we received a correction to this effect: It now reads as follows: "Impossibility of a democratic change over political power." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first sentence of that report of yours and paragraph, you say that the monopoly over information, the state television monopoly over information and to a lesser degree the national radio monopoly was a guarantee that Slobodan Milosevic would cash in on extraordinary political Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. royalties. Is that right? Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you conclude by saying that this media supremacy and how this -- this will pay off many -- many-fold prior to the elections, and the same would be repeated at the December 1992 elections. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, 1990 and 1992, that this will be repeated in December 1992 as well.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my questions are as follows: In response to a question from Mr. Nice during your examination-in-chief, you said that in Yugoslavia, that is to say in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, you arrived there in 1994 and that you dealt in journalism. And prior to the war in Kosovo, you published an article linked to propaganda. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in 1994 I directed a work on the media and hatred than I wrote an article on the impossibility of covering the war in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, I'm going to try and present you with facts. In view of the fact that you lived and worked in the former Yugoslavia for the period of time you did, were you aware of a notorious fact at the time, namely that the Albanians in Kosovo did not go out to the elections to vote for a whole decade, and quite certainly they did not in 1990 and 1992. Did you know about this undisputed fact, the fact that the Albanians did not go to the polls?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know about that, something like that, and you spent so much time there? Can you compare, for example, the propaganda you discussed in your report with the propaganda that was used, utilised in order to have people not go to the elections at all, not go to vote? And it is a fact that the Albanians did not go to vote for ten years. But the important years for me that I'd like to focus on is 1990 and 1992. So did you hear about the propaganda that lead out to the fact that the Albanians took no part in Serbia's political life at all.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make a clarification. I began to work in 1994. I made -- prepared a comparative study on the use of propaganda and the propagation of ethnic hatred. I worked on that from 1994 to 1995. And then in 1996 I published another article. I never said that I spent a -- many years in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, I have to hurry this up a little. Now, why I'm asking you this is because you conclude, you observe in paragraph 111 titled "Impossibility of a democratic changeover of a political power," you make a conclusion there. Now, let me take you through 1992. You mentioned Milan Panic, for example, who in 1992 was a counter-candidate to Slobodan Milosevic. Slobodan Milosevic, as far as I recall, got a few more votes, although ten years -- that was ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a million. A million more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, a million more. So quite a substantial difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know that the democratic opposition in Serbia in 1992 already had solid foundations, it had a good response among the people? What it did came across a good response from the population. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You referred to two elections, 1990 and 1992. I would like to go back to the purpose of the paragraph 111. Here I am referring to the media coverage of the December 1990 elections during which the opposition did not have a fair access to the audio-visual media of the state. I remind you that television is the main news medium for the vast majority of the Serbian people, and so there was an inequality, and I'm referring to the study that was prepared, "Television and elections in Serbia" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've explained all that. Mr. De la Brosse, you've explained all that in your report. I'm not asking you to repeat what you've explained in the report. You spoke about the influence of the authorities on the elections and you don't know the notorious facts that the Albanians in 1990 did not go to the polls. But I'm not interested in that either. What I'm interested in is this: Had the Albanians gone out to the elections in 1992 would the authorities have remained in power? Would Slobodan Milosevic himself have remained in power? Can you answer that question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Albanians gone out to vote, there would have been a million votes added to Milan Panic's vote. Pure arithmetic would have shown that had they wanted to have a parliamentary struggle, Slobodan Milosevic and the authorities would not have been able to stay if power?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will move on to another subject, but I think this is quite obvious and self-evident, but it is up to you to assess, of course. I have just broached the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, something else. What you state in paragraph 68. And we dealt at length on the issue. It is as you said the paranoia of conspiracy, I think you called it. And in you first statement, you say: "However, what set Serbian nationalism far apart was its paranoia." That's right, isn't it? That's what you say?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph, paragraph 69, and you've already spoken about that too, you mentioned Dobrica Cosic and say that when he was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and you quote his words, "it is a question of a total war being waged against our nation," and you wind up by invoking the influence of the mass media. Are you referring to the mass media with respect to the world information media?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you indicate the passage again, please?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is paragraph 69, the last sentence. Just before paragraph 70.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that he's speaking about the international media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, yes. Now take a look at paragraph 75, if you would, the beginning of paragraph 75. And you say: "When despite everything certain information directly implicating Serbian responsibility for the perpetuation of atrocities managed to filter through, it was distorted. On the 27th of May, 1992, 17 inhabitants of Sarajevo were killed by a Serbian shell, and 150 wounded as they were queueing for bread. The picture of the massacre would be broadcast by RTS only with the Serb's official version of events later on, which accused the Sarajevo government of having organised it to cause the West to intercede." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I say is that on Serbian television, the only thing shown was one version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you know that the whole of Serbia was watching this on that day and that the citizens of Serbia watched with horror these images that were broadcast? You don't know about that, that they were horrified?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me reread this, please. So what was your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to go back to the question. If you didn't understand it, I have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like at this point to open up several questions dealt with by Mr. de la Brosse which in the future work related to Bosnia -- actually, he analysed what happened in Vasa Miskin Street. I think this will be of great importance to Your Honours. That is my opinion, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I would like to ask the witness before that. Before I go on to Vasa Miskin Street and the event there, does he know at all, he can just give me a yes or no answer, whether he knows of the existence of the American agency for relations with the public Norton Hill, and Ruder and Fin. Has he heard of those two agencies? If he deals in propaganda and is testifying before us in court here --

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are allude to go an American agency which Mr. Parenti talks about in his book?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm just asking you whether you know of the existence of those two agencies, Norton Hill and Ruder and Fin, and that they lobbied for the Bosnian and Croatian side. Are you aware of that? Do you know about that? Do you have knowledge of that? Give me a yes or no answer, please?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on French television in 1993 given the fact that you deal in propaganda, did you hear a statement made by James Harf and I'm just going to read several sentences, just give me a yes or no answer once again please. "It is not up to us to check out the truthfulness of information. We are not capacitated to do so. What is our task is to disseminate useful information as soon as possible. Independently of that, the Croatian and Muslim past were such that they were coloured by strong anti-Semitism. Dozens of thousands of Jews were killed in concentration camps and everything spoke in favour of the fact that intellectuals and the Jewish organisations would be hostilely disposed towards the Croats and Bosnians. For us this was a challenge to have this position changed at its very roots. For us, this was a great success, magnificent success. When the Jewish organisations stood on the side of Bosnian organisations, we were able to equate the Serbs straight away in public" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "The Nazis."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What do you see in your control as amicus the purpose of this question? How is it of assistance or how are you trying to assist the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that I would use concrete examples to link all this up, because Mr. de la Brosse spoke about Vasa Miskin Street, the incident there, and how that fact, what happened there was assessed in Serbia. And these will be things that you will be dealing with many times in times to come. And let me tell you why. He doesn't know about this statement. All right. I'm satisfied the answer and it will be useful to you. But do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you going to put -- very simply, is this the point of it all, that there was manipulation of propaganda by Bosnians or Croats? Is that the point that you're making?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. I stated the quotation by Mr. de la Brosse that Dobrica Cosic said there was a conspiracy afoot against the Serbs than the world media were used for that purpose, harnessed for that purpose, and it is along those lines that I am examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Isn't that really a matter for Mr. Milosevic to put forward? Is it really a matter for the amicus to get into this kind of argument? Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I may be of assistance. Mr. Milosevic actually put forward these arguments when he referred to a person, Merlinot who appeared and made such allegations, and he actually quoted quite lengthy the same things that Mr. Tapuskovic puts now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I seem to remember the quotation attributed to Mr. Harf. Yes. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we must ask you to move on. These are matters which Mr. Milosevic has already raised. We are familiar with the argument, and it's not going to assist us to have it reiterated. And time is short. We really have a limit on the time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I won't go back to that issue, no, but the three events that he mentions in his report I would have to put forward to you here and also to hear his comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 27th of May, 1992, in the bread line a shell killed all these people and 150 were wounded, 150 wounded and 17 inhabitants killed? Is that correct? And that's what you say in your report, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also true and correct that all the world agencies carried this news item that day and on the following days, that they repeated this many times? Is that true as well?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that the media and the international agencies gave information about the massacre, reported on the massacre, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also true and correct that on that same day in Lisbon, negotiations were interrupted between the three national delegations which were discussing the constitutional order to come? They began on the 21st of May, the Portuguese Ambassador, Cutileiro, the presiding officer interrupted the conference on that very day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true and correct that on the 30th of May, a Security Council decision was taken on 757 Resolution introducing sanctions against the FRY, Serbia and Montenegro. Is that true? Did the United Nations Security Council make that decision without previously ascertaining who was responsible for the incident in the first place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point of reiterating all this, Mr. Tapuskovic? I want to know what the point is and I have not got it. What are you going to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you will be able to ascertain the truth here about Racak, for instance. You are going to decide on what happened in Racak, whether it was civilians who were killed or something else. Here before public opinion, international public opinion, the news was put forward that the crime was committed by the Serbs. Now, Mr. de la Brosse is here. Was it ever established who used and deployed the shell? Whereas what followed the incident was sanctions imposed against Serbia. So that is the point of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We've heard this argument before. You're suggesting that it was the Bosnians who were responsible. This witness isn't to deal with that. He's merely dealing with propaganda. And we've heard all these arguments. We hear them from the accused all the time. Now, you must consider your role as amicus and consider that you're not putting forward a positive case on behalf of anybody. And I must ask you to finish this -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I must ask you to finish this in the next ten minutes, by quarter past.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will finish whenever you want me to, but I must say quite seriously that I'm constantly under time constraints, and it is very difficult for me to perform my role as amicus curiae. So I ask myself whether I am necessary to the Trial Chamber in this case at all. I cannot work under pressure of this kind. And let me say also -- I have to say this although maybe it's not the right place, but I am the oldest person here and I can't be under stress constantly as to be given instruction when and what to ask. If I can't raise issues of this kind, then my services serve no purpose here. It has nothing to do with Mr. Milosevic here, but it has to do with questions that you will have to deliberate about and make a ruling on. If I'm superfluous here, then I no longer wish to perform this role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Go on to your next point, provided it's not going over old ground which we've covered already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the occurrence of the 5th of February, 1994, the Markale incident. Sixty-eight dead in that incident in Sarajevo. On that particular day, the truth is disseminated for Markale, the first Markale incident. In 1996, it was established that this was really perpetrated by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These points are all made by Mr. Milosevic. It's not helpful to have them reiterated with this witness. No doubt we'll have to make a decision about it. This witness can't help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me really shorten what I wanted to say. I wanted to raise a topic here, and that is this: It was stated that Cosic and the Academy of Arts and Sciences, that they were constantly putting out certain information as to a Serb conspiracy or, rather, an international conspiracy. That's what de la Brosse speaks about. I just wanted to raise this question, that before anything was established, certain steps were taken against certain states. I, of course, know that you can not establish that at this point in time. You'll clear it up at the end. But before the truth was known about anything, certain actions were taken on the part of the international state against -- community against that state. And that's the question I wanted to raise. And this was done on three occasion up until the bombings, which did not wait for a decision as to what had happened at the Markale 3 incident, but I don't want to go back to that. I want to end by raising a question we had here already and which refers to propaganda. You will recall, I'm sure, that with witness Jeri Laber, for example, I broached a particular question which had to do with propaganda precisely because in December 1992, the Muslim leaders in Bosnia accused the Bosnian Serbs of raping 50.000 Muslim women in camps where they held them as detainees, as prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about that? Do you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to a witness who appeared at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to a testimony. But I'm asking you whether you know about this, these facts and figures. And they are contained in a document that was already raised here in court, and it has been tendered into evidence, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had access to that testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about that piece of information or not? Did you read in Newsweek that 30 to 50.000 rapes this had been committed by Serb soldiers, that this was put out before the sanctions were imposed?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that at the time. I learnt it from Mr. Parenti's book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was one of the arguments before the sanctions were imposed against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's nothing to do with this witness why sanctions were imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know that there was even a report by the Council of Europe that was put out which speaks about the rape of 20.000 Muslim women. And after that, the International Red Cross made a statement by Philippe Miserez which said there was no evidence that camps of that kind of existed or ever existed. He stresses that the greatest part of prisoners of war were held in Bosnia by all sides and there were 10.000 in July 1992 and the accusations were exaggerated. Do you know about that? Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned it in Mr. Parenti's book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I refer to another topic? But I don't know whether I'll be able to complete it within the space of three or four minutes. Can I start my third topic or shall I give up on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can start it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 96, you speak about the fact that the Serbs or, rather, the Serbia authorities via radio and television Serbia played the nationalistic card as it says here and the air raids were considered to be an international conspiracy against Serbia. That's what you state here. And a little further on you go on to say the following, that even the least collateral damage for which responsibility was taken over by the allied aviation, air force, was exploited by the media, and the target was inside and outside to strengthen the idea that it really was a war against the civilian population. That is what you write in your report.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 96, I can find it, but I don't see the second part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 97, that is, the middle of the paragraph. No, 98. I'm sorry, it's paragraph 98 that I'm referring to and they mostly said that a F170 American aeroplane was shot down and that this was exaggerated and exploited, the slightest collateral damage caused by NATO aircraft was exploited for external and internal consumption, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, what is the question, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question with reference to this is: Is it exaggeration or were bridges and refineries and hydro electric power plants destroyed, and to take the lowest figure, 502 civilians were killed? Is that correct, to take a conservative figure? Did you have information of that kind working on your report, compiling it?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What figure are you alluding to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, again, what counsel is putting, and it really is a Defence point is that again this is an exaggeration because there were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. indeed -- there was damage and there were casualties on the Serb side. Could you briefly deal with it, please, Mr. de la Brosse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quote the example of the American aircraft, the 11 -- the F170. It's not sure that it was shot down by the -- whether it was shot down or whether it was an accident, that American F170 stealth bomber. And this was presented as a victorious exploit by the Serbian army. I'm asking for a little bit of time here because I feel that the -- I'm -- the amicus curiae is a bit stressed. So am I, in fact. It's hard to answer just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's adjourn. Now you, you must bring this to an end, Mr. Tapuskovic as quickly as possible, because time is limited and in my judgement these are all Defence points and I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I need two more minutes. Two more minutes and I'll be finished. I'll give up all the other questions. I just want to clarify this point otherwise there's no sense in working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't want people to be stressed though. You can ask two minutes more then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what I would want to ask you, Mr. de la Brosse. Is the principle -- is it the principle of every democratic country to have the freedom of the press, the freedom of the media and for the media to be able to freely express themselves and put forward things to the public even if they are not always correct or the truth? Is that a principle that prevails in all countries throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Freedom of the press is put forward as the cornerstone of freedom in a democratic society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's how I understand it too. Now, do you know this, that in Yugoslavia, the director of the television was convicted to a prison term of ten years because he failed to liberate the -- failed to evacuate the television building when the television building and station was bombed? Now, I'm not going into that matter. He got ten years of a prison sentence for that. Now, what could have justified, this is what I'm interested in, that the symbol of democracy, a television station in any country should be hit by a NATO shell and that 17 civilians were killed in the process. That is my question to you. If freedom of the media is a democratic principle, how is that possible then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a matter for the witness to answer. Yes. Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it may be in the particular circumstances you could forego any re-examination and the witness can be allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour, I actually have a few points that need to be clarified, and it's -- because it relates to the articles that the witness was supposed to read. It relates to one item with the 41 children, and one point in relation to his methodology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, in the cross-examination, both the accused and Mr. Tapuskovic put to you various events and classifications of personalities or groups, suggesting that these were true, these facts were true, and challenging your findings that this was propaganda. My question to you is: Effective propaganda, is that simply spreading lies or can the reporting of true facts be even more effective as a propaganda tool?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that one is reporting facts that actually happened can be very -- can also be a very effective means of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, the accused challenged the validity of your expertise as such given your working methods, and you yourself actually addressed limitations, particularly the lack of knowledge of the Serbian language and details of historical facts. You said in this regard that this did not allow you to see all facets of that propaganda at work and that, therefore, you could not reconstitute the entire scope of the propaganda. This fact that you could not see all facets, would that work in favour of the accused or would it be his disadvantage, your limitations?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would be disadvantageous to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the material itself, the body of material used. As I said, I limited myself to -- to using certain newspapers like Politika, material which basically was used to analyse the media and television coverage, especially the major Serbian television news programme. As I was saying on Monday, there were many other areas which are used in order to get propaganda across which were not studied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, I was actually referring to the knowledge of the Serbian language and the lack of all the details of all the history. Would that -- that therefore you could not see all facets in propaganda. Would that disadvantage him or would that even work in favour of him?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that I do not know the Serbian language, I know a little bit about history but I'm not an historian, as I've said, all of that meant that I was unable to study the use that might have been made of certain symbols or certain emblems, and that, therefore, is a limitation on the study of the propaganda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have read, I understood, the articles that were given to you by the accused, and you have already mentioned that you had difficulties to comment on these articles and even found that they were incorrect in relation to an article in the German language or, rather, the Swiss language.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have to inform and everybody should know that here in court, that the source of this document is actually a document provided to the US embassy by Momcilo Krajisnik on the 14th of April, 1997, in Pale. Mr. Milosevic did not know that, so he should also know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to put to the witness another. The Prosecution has tried to find the underlying articles, and I would like to put to Mr. de la Brosse another example of the underlying article, and it's again in the German language because that was the easiest to do over the weekend. On and -- yes, please. I have provided the underlying article from Mr. Tuman in Die Zeit, and one of our German colleagues, I have to say it wasn't me, has found these quotes which are highlighted in this article and has translated these quotes. The first quote as Mr. Milosevic read from this document that he had at hand was that "out of 30.000 of the Serbs that used to live in Mostar, there are only 400 left." And the complete quote is actually reread. Author is referring to other articles that in 1992 and 1993, "Serbs expelled more than 50.000 Muslims and Croats from the Bosnian Prijedor at the same time out of 30.000 Serbs that used to live in Mostar, there are only 400 today." And the next quote that Mr. Milosevic did in relation to the refugees in Serbia, the complete quote is: "The Croatian -- in Croatia today live 550.000 refugees, expelled victims of ethnic cleansing, but also Serbs give home to 450.000 refugees victims of ethnic cleansing. Both are true." Then there is also the reference that Mr. Milosevic read here in relation to the warmongering journalism and is actually a quote referring to a dispute in the media, and it starts with "The reproach of the revisionists is," and then comes the quote. Did you yourself also find this article or find similar incorrect -- incorrect matters in these examples?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a bit uncomfortable about the type of excerpts that I was asked to comment on. I did some research on one article, and I didn't do any research for the other so I can't answer yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do any research on Alfred Sherman who also had a quote in this group of documents referring to the Germans wanting control over the Danube basin in the Balkans? Were you aware that in summer 1993 Alfred Sherman was residing in Pale next to Radovan Karadzic and actually was his advisor?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that should be enough. I could continue with more examples from this, but I think that's enough. And the only other thing that I actually want to address is the 41 children killed, allegedly killed, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have actually in paragraph 5 of your report commented the entire story with all the details, and I just want to refer you to this paragraph. And in the context -- in this context, the accused spoke about the disclaimer done by the Serbian television, and you have actually in footnote 13 given a quote -- you've quoted this disclaimer. And I just want to draw your attention to the following sentence: "Assuming the news story was not authentic, now we can't say whether it is or it is not because we have no convincing proof, and it's always easy to apologise," and so forth and so on. Is this a clear denial that the event didn't happen, or is there an underlying message in there to the contrary when you read this sentence? Haven't you found it? It's footnote 13.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm answering your question, but in the television excerpt that I'm referring to in footnote 13, the journalist says that "Assuming the news story was not authentic, [In English] ... Say whether it is or it is not." [Interpretation] The news was denied by the Reuters press agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll come back to the report. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had an objection earlier on, namely, you said that you could not accept these 100 pages which I provided on the previous day because the texts were not integral, that is the 100 pages were just extracts. But the witness explained that he looked for one article out of all those contained in those 100 pages. So I have two objections. The first is that I received all of those 100 pages from the side opposite. It was not I that found them. I received them, and I showed you the references of the opposite side regarding all of those 100 pages. If you don't accept that, then it means that the opposite side is giving me unacceptable documents which cannot be of any use. So this is a question that should be addressed, why they're doing it. And another argument in favour of what I'm saying is that the quotations of the witness contained in his would-be expert report are also incomplete or even in many cases they are parts of sentences taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let us save time -- let us save time on this. We will consider what the status of these documents is going to be, but meanwhile, let the witness retire. He shouldn't have to remain any longer for this kind of debate. Mr. de la Brosse, thank you for coming, and thank you for coming back to the Tribunal to continue your evidence. It is now finished, and you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will consider what the status of these documents is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit the various articles. So that is the first seven items in the index which I have in front of me. They will all be admitted. They are, of course, not evidence, but since the witness was dealing with what was in the press, on the same basis this can be admitted. We will not admit the book by Michael Parenti. It is not our practice, as we made plain during the course of the trial, to admit such document into evidence. Accordingly, numbers 1 to 7 admitted, the book not. But we can have exhibit number for those seven.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 141, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I raise two short administrative matters because I think everybody in the courtroom should know so that nobody prepares something in vain. The first thing is in light of the recent decision in relation to Professor Kristan, the witness will not appear this week, and we will reconsider whether he needs to be called. And in relation to the witness order, we would like to make one change, and that relates to the witness 47 and the witness B-1775, given the change in the court schedule and the practical reasons for travelling and so forth, we would like to have B-1775 before the Witness C-047. We believe that C-047 would then testify next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. There was one -- there was one witness who you weren't going to call. I can't remember who it was. It was announced last week. Perhaps you could at some stage let us have the number and pseudonym again. I have it. The registry, as usual, has it. Thank you. The next matter we need to consider are the various Rule 92 bis issues. I'll just get my papers into order. The witnesses were 1455, 1725, and Osman Selak. The first two were -- are cumulative in the sense they both deal with the takeover of Zvornik and, therefore, potentially admissible under Rule 92 bis, with cross-examination, of course. One matter of concern, though, Mr. Groome, is the fact that these statements are coming in late and requiring a variation of the Rule. That's not a practice which the Trial Chamber would encourage at all, if you can help us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, these were witnesses originally scheduled to testify viva voce and it was a decision by the Prosecution, who wanted to expedite matters here, wherever appropriate here we would seek wherever to 92 bis (B) the statements of such witnesses. We are making efforts to now complete all of the necessary paperwork and comply with all time limits of viva voce witnesses that will be called later in the case which we will attempt to do at least in part by 92 bis (D) but apologise for the short notice on these particular ones. It was inevitable in these particular situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if you've had an opportunity of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't know if you've had the opportunity, Mr. Groome, of reading the objections the amici about Osman Selak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would like to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's intention to only rely on approximately or less than half of the transcript, less than 400 pages. The Prosecution felt it was in fairness, just basic principles of fairness required that we seek to submit the entire transcript including the cross-examination rather than just the examination-in-chief that we would seek to rely upon. It's our position that even if the testimony of Mr. Selak were to be taken entirely viva voce, that it still would be necessary for the accused to read that 800-page transcript. So it's the Prosecution's position that we take no position on the -- on how much time is allotted the accused to -- that the Court determines is a reasonable period of time to cross-examine Mr. Selak, but in the interests of saving some time, it seems entirely appropriate to seek to introduce his prior court testimony before the Trial Chamber under 92 bis (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One point which is made by the amici relates to evidence concerning the relationship between the military and political wings of the government which it says is -- which is said is pivotal evidence and relates to the accused. Will that evidence be given live?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It was our intention to do some very small portion of that live but to again rely on the prior testimony simply in the interests of saving time. The Prosecution would not object to leading that evidence if that is the determination by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what parts of his evidence do you propose to give live so we have some idea of the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Portions of the testimony related to that pivotal relationship as well as some additional documents that are more relevant to the Court's consideration of this matter than the Chamber that's hearing the Brdjanin case. We anticipate that his testimony, if his prior testimony is accepted under 92 bis (D), that his viva voce testimony, that component of his evidence would be less than an hour of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Kay, you hear what's suggested for Mr. Selak if we take him first, that evidence about the acts and conduct or anything which remotely could be said to be the acts and conduct will be given live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One of the problems in dealing with his testimony in this way is that the two transcripts amount to a very dense quantity of material, 800 pages. And it's very difficult going through that material to have a clear understanding of all the detail of his evidence. It is possible to have an understanding of the generality, but the concern for my part was that this could be opening a door for future problems in the trial if the accused has not dealt with something that remains within those papers that is crucial to the Prosecution or becomes crucial at a later stage. If his evidence was given not in 92 bis form but in a simple and concise way so that the accused was able to understand the nature of the case against him, in my submission the stated objectives of the Prosecution could be readily achieved, avoiding a great morass of detail within those transcripts that it is difficult to get to grips with in relation to this case because, for instance, that evidence concerned the trial of General Talic. And we are being cautious about this matter because at first sight it seems the transcript is just being produced, albeit now cut in half to 400 pages, that in the end there will not be a very great saving of time if one has avoided taking these issues in a precise form viva voce before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter, isn't it, for the Prosecution? The point is that the evidence could all be repeated. The only thing of a transcript is that it is the evidence which was given live earlier. So if it's all repeated again, we'll be in the same position. And it's a matter for the Prosecution how they present their case, surely, not for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it is a matter for us because it deals with the ability of the other party to be able to comprehend the issues that are being put in the courtroom, which is a fair trial issue, and I would submit for the Judges themselves. Looking at that transcript, the meandering way of the evidence and questioning makes the points very difficult to follow, and I would urge the Trial Chamber, if they have not been in a position to do so yet, to spend a little time going through the transcript to have a look at that intelligibility issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In an ideal world, no doubt all the evidence could be given live in the way that you recommend, concentrating purely on the issues in a case. The problems that we are having in this Tribunal is the length of these cases. Now, I know that this is not your responsibility at all or indeed the responsibility of the accused. Of course not. It's the responsibility of the Prosecution, and they have to grapple with this. But at the same time, the Tribunal must do something to ensure that material is put in an expeditious and fair way, and this particular Rule is one of the ways of doing it. Here is a man who has given evidence twice, given his evidence in chief, and this is a way of getting that evidence in front of this Trial Chamber without going over it all again but making sure, from the point of view of a fair trial, that the accused has the opportunity to cross-examine. It's the scale and complexity of these trials which require the one forms new forms of thinking in the ways of conducting trials, away Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from the old common law oral model but, of course, ensuring that fairness is maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't disagree with that. And we are an international court here applying international rules of evidence. But the point I'm making is that in an ideal world, the original questioning would have been clear in its direction and the issues able to be comprehended. But the massive detail and the repetition of issues with slight developments at one stage from a stage that was given previously, relying upon various documents, do not make this evidence clear to understand, and that has been my concern on behalf of this accused. I appreciate the statement by the Trial Chamber then concerning the nature of these trials and the time taken upon them, but it does seem to me that the proceedings are helped better if there is concise and clear questioning that puts us directly into the issues, which can't take too long a period of time. But if one considers the approach we've had in relation to this submission, I appreciate the Prosecution are under pressure of work and time, but 800 pages turns up with a supporting application saying admit this into evidence and a general description of what is within those pages. We would have been far better served if we could have gone to that document, looked at certain pages and passages which perhaps encompass ten pages in one part, five in another, one in another, drawn red lines down the side and been able to say, "This is the issue within this testimony from this witness on that occasion and it is summed up in this form as being an issue that goes to structure and command responsibility." But that hasn't happened. So forgive me for being a Luddite on this matter, because we have to face what has been -- what has been done through the means presented, what has been attempted by the means presented. And that's where clarity of issues, in our submission, not only serve the accused but they also serve the Trial Chamber. And if we are to have a practice of vast pages of transcripts being produced under a Rule which is to help precious court time, it's going to cause great difficulties in isolating the issues in this case because we lose the focus in the case against this accused. Those are my submissions on the Selak transcript unless I can assist the Court any further on that particular one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Dealing first with 1455. Cumulative crime base, Zvornik, and not acts and conduct of the accused, I'm able to paraphrase it in that way because we know the territory that we're dealing with. The one extra issue I would raise on this evidence is that it deals with a particular distinct village called Drinjaca that I don't believe that we have had evidence about to date in this trial, and so in that sense, there is a fresh introduction of evidence on a particular place. I had been setting out an oral document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, are you saying that goes to the cumulative character of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The fact that it is a new village is a fresh place, so it could be said to be a distinct issue and is, therefore, not cumulative of evidence relating to the place. In the context of Zvornik as a whole, that is a different matter. But I raise that point for the Trial Chamber's consideration. I'm conscious of the fact that in the Croatia phase of the trial when we looked at this and we considered the Rule 92 bis applications that were cumulative of the Babic testimony, the Trial Chamber was happy to rule in those statements on the basis of generality of area rather than distinctly looking at particular villages. I was writing something over the weekend for the Trial Chamber on this, and I haven't had time to print it out and hand it in. If I can just check and see I've covered all the points. No. That's all I need to raise on 1455. 1775, I've had an opportunity to consider today. Again this is Zvornik crime base, cumulative of Zvornik events within Zvornik itself, not acts and conduct of the accused but deals with the mass burial of peoples around the area, and as yet, we have had no witness on evidence such as this. We have had pathologist evidence, but I think I'm right in saying that we have had no specific witness dealing with transportation of bodies from places and their burial. A factor that he does deal with that is important within the case, he mentions a Belgrade pathologist and his evidence concerning that particular matter and its relevance to issues outside Bosnia-Herzegovina are obviously relevant in the case against this accused. Now, the Trial Chamber, I anticipate, would permit cross-examination on this particular witness following the guidance that's been given from previous decisions. Outside what happens in Zvornik, it may well be that the Court, in exercising its discretion, would want to hear the live evidence concerning the shipment of the bodies and their disposal in various places, which is an important and distinct feature of this witness's testimony. Can I assist the Court any further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with the witness Mr. Selak and the proposal by the opposite side over there to accept 800 pages of transcript, the question is, in fact, whether or not what is being presented here in the courtroom before the public should be presented clearly or unclearly. As I understand it, the opposite side considers that this should be expressed in an unclear way, that is to say, to make it as confusing as possible that absolutely nobody can actually establish what it's all about. The transcripts from some kind of other trial, case, which has nothing to do with either the authorities of Serbia or myself personally, or indeed with the aspect from which we should view these events. So it does not provide any possibility of clarifying matters. There is some sort of cross-examination accorded here which is very suspect, of doubtful value, not only because I could, for example, claim that it was done in an incompetent way. I'm far from making any judgements as to anybody's capabilities or competence. That's something I don't want to do. But if it targets a specific act, trial, or behaviour on the part of an individual, somebody that we're dealing with here, then it did not have as its focus a whole scale of general questions which relate to the events that took place in Bosnia and a context -- the context in which those events took place, the circumstances which from the aspect of a rational-minded and may I say honest and reasonable approach to these events must be clarified, because we're dealing here with an individual case, the transcript of which for the examination in chief and cross-examination is to be introduced without any - how shall I put this? - physical possibility of delving into the contents of it before the individual appears, before the witness appears at all. I, therefore, consider that this option to use lack of clarity in presenting this whole case, the whole case that the witness is to testify about, in my opinion is something that is quite contrary to the basic principles of behaviour in courts throughout the world, courts which are legal courts. And as for these two other individuals, Mr. Kay has already indicated that with 1455 there are new facts to be disclosed and 1725, or 1755, I don't remember the number exactly. I didn't jot the number down, but once again that we have new facts coming to light there too. So I don't know how you're going to go about this, how this written testimony is going to be in order to make the trial an expeditious one are going to be accepted without having a necessary, if I can put it that way, a necessary explanation, one that is required if you do indeed feel that this is testimony that should be heard, that merits being heard from the person who has come here to testify. Therefore, I think that we are going to infringe upon the general principles in both cases, and I categorically oppose having this introduced under Rule 92 bis. And as Mr. Kay has said here, these are new facts coming to light and not cumulative testimony and cumulative evidence. And I think that with Selak I have put forward sufficient arguments to prove my point. Now, whether it is cumulative or not, that is once again a relative concept, because for you anything can become cumulative. You are accusing Serbia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia here, myself personally for the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the war in Croatia as well. So from that standpoint, all the testimonies are cumulative. And from that point of view, all of them could come under 92 bis rulings because none of them have direct contacts and links to me or the authorities in Serbia. So they fully succumb under your rules, fall under your rules. Then we ask ourselves the question for what you need your witnesses anyway, and why you need these individual cases at all which prove the existence of something that does not in fact exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly. It is the Prosecution's desire and intention to present the evidence quite clearly and it is our position that it is no less clear because it is in written form or from a previous trial. With respect to shortcomings of earlier cross-examiners, the Prosecution as I said earlier is not opposing the accused being given a full and fair opportunity to cross-examine the witness and the Prosecution's producing the witness here for that purpose. Finally or -- not finally, but with respect to cumulative -- issue of cumulativeness, 92 bis (A)(i)(a) describes cumulative as one of the factors the chamber should consider. It is the Prosecution's position that although it is a very important factor it is not dispositive of the issue. Furthermore, the importance of whether an issue -- evidence is cumulative is less important in cases where the witness will be here to testify and -- or will be here to be cross-examined and can answer any question regarding written assertions made in the written statement. And finally, Your Honour, I asked a colleague of mine who was working on the Selak transcript earlier today to examine the transcript and -- with a view towards identifying those sections of the transcript which we will not be placing great importance on and those sections which are of critical importance. I have some notes here before me. I would propose that the Prosecution turn this into a letter sent to the accused and the amici via the registrar, and it would identify those portions of the transcript on which are -- we would seek to focus on those which we would not. The Prosecution is also willing to provide a draft summary of the anticipated live testimony to assist both the amici and the accused in their preparation for this important witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will consider these matters. Yes. Have you got your witness here? We might as well use what time we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution recalls Witness B-024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-024, if you'd like to take a seat. I'm sorry that we haven't been able to get to your evidence earlier and also because the courtroom is required, we shall only be able to have a short period of your evidence today, and we'll have to ask you to come back tomorrow. Perhaps, Mr. Groome, you can take a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Groome: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B-024, at the end of last week you were describing a visit, the second visit of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic to the Zvornik municipality. I have a few more questions I would like to ask you about that visit. The first question is how long altogether was she present in the Zvornik municipality on the second visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that altogether she was there for three to four hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for us all of the places in Zvornik municipality that you know she visited on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, she just visited Zvornik, and that was under Serb control already, and Mali Zvornik where the Serbs were too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe with any greater particularity the places that she visited in Zvornik? You've told us she was at the Alhos centre. Can you tell us any we are places she may have gone that day that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was there with her when she was in Mali Zvornik and in the Alhos building. However, afterwards, she was escorted by the police and she toured Zvornik, which was already under the control of the Serb forces. So I don't know exactly what individual places in the town of Zvornik she visited, but I think she went to the hospital, among others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if she had any meetings with any members of the Yugoslav People's Army on this second visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the end of May 1992, the time after the Yugoslav People's Army officially withdrew from Bosnia, and my question to you is: After their official withdrawal from Bosnia, were you aware of any involvement of the now renamed Yugoslav army in Bosnia after May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After May 1992, it is common knowledge that in 1993 in an operation that a unit from Valjevo under the command of a certain officer named Solaja took part in an operation in Zvornik itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what type of unit Colonel Solaja commanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was a tank unit from the Valjevo garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many tanks were in this unit that fought in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know those details, but it was general knowledge that the unit, in 1993, did take part in a battle near Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you came to know who was paying Vinko Pandurevic's salary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a time, I was the president of the Executive Board, and I know that at the time he received his salary from the TO, the Territorial Defence. And he told me that he also received a salary from the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time he told you that he received a salary from the Yugoslav army, what organisation or what formation did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know details like that, which unit he belonged to, but I think it was common knowledge that the active officers were on the salary lists of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vinko Pandurevic was an officer in what army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an officer in the Army of Republika Srpska. But before that, he had been a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, some unit which withdrew from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the official withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army, did there come a time when you became aware that military supplies from the Yugoslav army, as it was then called, were being brought into Zvornik from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any concrete evidence of this, but I know that trucks from my company were engaged for the Defence Ministry's requirements, and I know that the drivers went to the territory of Yugoslavia to bring in logistical equipment for the army. However, I don't know what kind of material this was and what the quantities involved were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what period of time were these trucks that you've referred to being used to transport logistical equipment in for the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were used throughout the whole war. As there was a state of war generally, the Defence Ministry always had the priority in requisition or using these trucks as compared to their use for commercial purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say for the entire war, are you saying for the time period between 1992 and the implementation of the Dayton Accord in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just testified that these trucks were requisitions by the Defence Ministry. The Defence Ministry of what country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Defence Ministry of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. May. The witness said that the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska had priority in the use of transport, the means of transport, and Mr. Groome says when did the ministry of -- when the Ministry of Defence requisitioned trucks. So that's quite contrary to what the witness was saying. The trucks belong to the company that he mentioned, and the purpose -- defence purposes were given the priority. The trucks were not requisitioned by the Defence Ministry, as far as I understood it. So the question is a leading one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you clarify exactly what happened to the trucks? What was the relationship between the Defence Ministry of Republika Srpska and these trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in a company which was in Republika Srpska, and during the war situation, we -- the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska had the priority to engage those trucks for logistical needs of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with what frequency did the Republika Srpska Defence Ministry engage these trucks for the purposes you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period I worked in the transport company, very frequently. And in fact, there were always two or three vehicles which were at the disposal of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some sense of the capacity of the type of truck that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the classical type of truck with about 20 kilogrammes -- 20 tons of bearing capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to ask you a more particular question regarding the frequency, could you estimate in times per week or times per month these trucks were used by the RS Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was roughly at least almost every day two or three trucks were placed at the disposal of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of how these trucks would cross from Zvornik into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the very beginning of the war, there was always a procedure at the border. So they probably applied the regular procedure. I didn't drive the trucks. I was the manager of that enterprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the procedure that was employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A classical customs procedure. There were customs records that were kept already at that time and goods coming from Yugoslavia going to Republika Srpska and vice versa as far as I can remember didn't have to pay customs duty but there were customs records kept because of taxation requirements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that for the trucks that you've described here that there should be records existing for every time they crossed the border between Serbia and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that, but I think that as soon as the drivers were mobilised by the Ministry of Defence they were treated as soldiers from then on. So they didn't bring in any documents to their original company, so that those documents are probably with the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can I now ask you to turn your attention to the relationship between the Republic of Serbia Ministry of Interior beyond and the Serbian Republic Ministry of Interior. Can I ask you to describe what you know about the relationship between those two entities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I was in the police at the very beginning of the conflict in Zvornik, we had good and friendly relations with the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, and we had logistic support to the extent which those police stations on the border between Mali Zvornik and Zvornik could assist us. And as a citizen, I do know that throughout the duration of the war, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska had good relations with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to the start of the conflict. Can you please describe in greater detail the logistical support that you and members of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska received from Serbia? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since according to plan B as a minority municipality we had a local police station in Karakaj in the Alhos building, we didn't have the technical equipment, I mean, the uniforms, the clothing that in those days were the same as in Yugoslavia, as in Serbia. So we received aid in the form of uniforms, some communications equipment from police stations in Mali Zvornik and Loznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the latter party of the conflict, did you receive any logistical support from the Serbian Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-024 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of April, I left the police, so I don't know how that cooperation developed later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think the time now is up. We must vacate the court. We will sit again tomorrow at 9:00. Witness B-024, could you be back please, at 9:00 tomorrow morning. If you would just wait a moment, we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of May, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
